title: The Zahiris
hookLine: the literalist school of Ibn Hazm, now small

lines: NO DOGS. IN COMES A WOLF.
cards: A sign on a park gate says: no dogs. Someone walks in with a pet wolf. Is that allowed?
One kind of reader reaches for the purpose behind the sign and says no, obviously. Another kind stops and asks: who decides what the sign meant beyond what it says?
If the rule-maker wanted wolves kept out, couldn't the rule-maker have written it? That second reader isn't being silly. That reader is protecting the text from everyone's guesses.
In Islamic law, that reader had a school, and its great voice lived in Muslim Spain. Today, the Zahiris.

teach.h: ZAHIR: WHAT SHOWS ON THE SURFACE.
teach.b: Zahir is Arabic for what's outward, what shows on the surface. The Zahiris are the people of the plain sense: the law is what the Qur'an and the sunnah actually say, read in their apparent meaning.
Tradition names Dawud al-Zahiri of Baghdad as the founder. Next, the tool they put down.
Other schools use qiyas, analogy: if wine is forbidden because it intoxicates, so is any drink that intoxicates. The Zahiris refused analogy as a source of law. Where the texts speak, follow them.
Where they're silent, the matter is left open, and no jurist may close it with a guess. Then their great voice.
Ibn Hazm of Cordoba wrote the method out at full length, in a book of law called al-Muhalla, arguing case by case.
Tradition remembers him as sharp-tongued and fearless in debate, and he also wrote a book about love, The Ring of the Dove, full of lovers, glances and letters. Last, a test case.
The Qur'an tells children, about aging parents, in Pickthall's words, "say not 'Fie' unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word."

An analogist says: if even 'fie' is forbidden, striking a parent is forbidden all the more. A Zahiri agrees on the result, not the route. The same verses already command kindness, and other texts forbid harm.
The plain sense is enough. The school is small today, but its question still sits in classrooms of fiqh: are you reading the text, or reading yourself into it?

how: Zahiri jurists derive law only from the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and sunnah, rejecting analogy (qiyas); the school is small today, but Ibn Hazm's books are still read by students of law.

o: a Spanish school devoted to poetry about love
a school that reads the law by the plain sense of the texts
a school that fills silent texts by careful analogy

p: the school's great voice, in Cordoba

s: the Zahiris use analogy to fill the gaps in the texts
they refused analogy; where the texts are silent, the matter stays open.
Ibn Hazm also wrote a book about love
The Ring of the Dove, full of lovers, glances and letters.
a Zahiri would allow striking a parent because the verse only forbids saying 'fie'
the same verses command kindness and gracious words, and other texts forbid harm; the result is the same, the route differs.

games.q: you're a Zahiri jurist. a question comes up that no verse or report addresses. an analogist offers a ruling by comparison. what do you say?
o: leave the matter open, since the texts are silent.
games.why: for the Zahiris, silence in the texts leaves a matter open. a jurist's comparison can't add a rule the texts didn't make.

practice: Take one short message you got recently, a text, an email, a note on the fridge, and read it once exactly as written, nothing added.

Then read it again with everything you know about the person who sent it, and notice the gap between the two readings, and how much of the second one you supplied yourself. If you pray, you can ask to read well.

wordCard.voice: The Zahiris. The school of the plain sense: the law is what the texts outwardly say, with no analogy to fill their silences. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Zahiris, from zahir, outward, apparent.

carryVoice: Your line: the plain sense. The words come first, and the guessing after. See you tomorrow.
